strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: improving code generation for low-resource programming languages without requiring model retraining
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model families (Qwen, Llama3, GPT-4o mini, DeepSeek), sizes, and benchmarks with proper statistical significance testing
Consistent performance improvements, particularly for smaller models with larger language performance gaps (e.g., 69.5% improvement on Lua for Qwen1.5B)
Clear methodology with well-articulated insight that test cases serve as language-agnostic functional knowledge transfer media
Practical implementation with detailed algorithm specification, comprehensive ablation studies, and thoughtful analysis of computational costs with optimization strategies
Demonstrates generalizability across three target languages (Lua, C++, Java) and compatibility with other test-time scaling methods
weaknesses: Limited novelty and incremental contribution: applying existing test-time scaling ideas (test case execution, multi-temperature sampling) to low-resource PLs without substantial methodological innovation

Insufficient analysis of test case quality and coverage: no validation that majority-voted test cases are correct, no metrics on test case coverage or distribution, no evidence test cases capture complex edge cases adequately
Fundamental limitation for stronger models: performance improvements diminish significantly for state-of-the-art models (DeepSeek: 7.4%, 2.2%, 4.9%), limiting applicability as models improve
Method depends critically on high-resource PL quality: systematic errors in Python code generation translate to incorrect test oracles, but correctness validation is not provided
Substantial computational overhead remains (28.81s average, 21.6× slower than vanilla), which may limit practical adoption despite being 5.65× faster than S*

Limited evaluation scope: only three target languages tested (Lua, C++, Java), with C++ and Java not truly low-resource; no evaluation on genuinely exotic languages; temperature settings (0, 0.7, 0.9, 1.1) claimed 'universally applicable' but lack principled justification
Low absolute performance on harder benchmarks (Ag-LiveCodeBench-X) raises questions about real-world utility; no error analysis or case studies of failure modes
Missing implementation details: timeout handling, output parsing language-specificity, test case generation failure rates, and exact definition of validity criteria

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: CodeLLMs perform inconsistently across programming languages, limiting real-world usability
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (7 different variants), benchmarks (3 distinct), and programming languages with proper statistical significance testing
Clear and intuitive core insight that test cases serve as language-agnostic transfer media for functional knowledge
Consistent improvements demonstrated across diverse settings, with particularly strong gains on Lua (up to 69.5%)
Includes ablation studies validating key components (multi-temperature sampling, voting strategy) and explores integration with other test-time methods
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines well-established techniques (Best-of-N sampling, multi-temperature inference, majority voting) without introducing fundamentally new concepts

Unfair baseline comparisons: compares against single-language test-time scaling methods (S*, LLM Judge) rather than comparable cross-language transfer approaches like Bridge-C, TransCoder-ST, or MultiPLT

Critical methodological concerns: (1) majority voting for test oracles can propagate consensus errors, (2) temperature values appear arbitrary with no justification, (3) fallback to greedy decoding frequency not analyzed
Weak generalization: strong results limited to Lua; improvements on C++/Java are modest (2.2%-51.7%), and for state-of-the-art models (DeepSeek) gains are marginal (2-7%)

Insufficient analysis of when/why the method works: no error analysis showing failure cases, no investigation of language-specific execution challenges, results don't generalize well to better-resourced languages

Limited scope of 'low-resource' language evaluation: only Lua is truly low-resource; C++ and Java are widely-used languages. No evaluation on other genuinely low-resource languages (Go, Rust, Haskell, Lisp)
Significant computational overhead remains: 21× slower than vanilla despite improvements, which is particularly unjustified for the modest gains on strong models

Missing critical implementation details: language-specific I/O handling, compilation vs. runtime error distinction, actual prompts used (Appendix D only shows templates), execution environment configuration

Incomplete related work: no experimental comparison with mentioned baselines (Bridge-C, TransCoder-ST, MultiPLT); insufficient engagement with program synthesis literature on test-based search (CEGIS)

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: performance gaps across programming languages in CodeLLMs
Elegant and intuitive core insight: test cases serve as language-agnostic medium for functional knowledge transfer
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple benchmarks, diverse models (8 variants), three target languages, statistical significance testing with t-tests (p<0.05)
Consistent improvements across models and languages, with particularly strong gains on smaller models (69.5% on Lua with Qwen1.5B) and meaningful gains even on state-of-the-art models
Ablation studies demonstrating value of multi-temperature hedged sampling and multi-sample voting for test oracle generation
Practical considerations addressed: time cost analysis, investigation of cost reduction strategies, demonstration of compatibility with other test-time scaling methods (S*)
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, detailed algorithm description, and reproducible implementation details including prompts in appendix
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: individual components (multi-temperature sampling, majority voting, execution-based selection) are standard; primary contribution is their combination for cross-lingual transfer, which is somewhat incremental
High computational overhead not adequately addressed: 21-28× slower than vanilla baseline, 16× slower for C++, limiting practical deployment despite being faster than S*

Insufficient analysis of knowledge transfer mechanism: no investigation of which problem types benefit most, when method fails, or how test case quality affects performance; missing error analysis and case studies

Test case generation has unexamined assumptions: relies on deterministic code execution, no analysis of false positive/negative rates in majority voting, timeout handling and precision tolerances not specified, choice of n=10 samples unjustified
Dependence on high-resource PL quality not rigorously examined: what happens when Python itself performs poorly? No analysis of test oracle accuracy or failure modes when high-resource language fails

Limited evaluation on truly low-resource languages: Lua is relatively mature; C++ and Java are not low-resource; results on languages like Rust, Kotlin, or domain-specific languages would strengthen claims

Temperature configuration lacks rigorous justification: specific temperatures (0, 0.7, 0.9, 1.1) with counts (1,3,3,3) appear ad-hoc; claims of 'universal applicability' unsupported; marginal improvements in ablation (Table 4); no sensitivity analysis
Missing important baseline comparisons: Bridge-C not compared (implementation difficulty insufficient justification), MultiPLT not compared; limits ability to assess relative contribution

Potential overfitting to test cases: selection purely based on n=10 test case pass rates; no discussion of distribution shift or whether generated test cases cover full problem space; no analysis of negative transfer

Limited statistical analysis: only 5 random seeds on selected models; high-variance scenarios and strong models lack sufficient rigor; no confidence intervals provided; Ag-LiveCodeBench-X shows very low baselines (2.8-36.5) raising meaningfulness questions

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MultiPL-E, Ag-LiveCodeBench-X), model families (Qwen, Llama, GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3), and target languages (Lua, C++, Java, R, Julia) with statistical significance testing
Substantial and consistent improvements particularly for smaller models and larger capability gaps (up to 69.5% on Lua), demonstrating practical utility
Computationally efficient uncertainty-aware adaptive selection mechanism achieving ~2× fewer tokens and ~4× faster execution than S* while maintaining accuracy
Well-motivated problem addressing real performance gaps in low-resource programming language code generation, with practical training-free solution
Thorough ablation studies and supplemental analyses (hyperparameter sensitivity, failure analysis, generalization to additional languages and source PLs)
Clear presentation with well-designed figures, detailed algorithm descriptions, and comprehensive appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (multi-temperature sampling, test-case-based selection, clustering for uncertainty) rather than introducing fundamentally new ideas; uncertainty estimation via simple cluster counting (Eq. 2) is straightforward

Fundamental dependence on high-resource language performance acts as hard ceiling; failure analysis (Table 13) shows 78-97% conditional failure when Python reference is incorrect, severely limiting applicability for weak high-resource languages

Hyperparameter choices lack principled justification: temperature values {0, 0.7, 0.9, 1.1}, clustering thresholds (δ_ext=1, δ_ast=2), and test case count (n=10) appear manually tuned with limited sensitivity analysis across models and languages

Modest improvements for state-of-the-art models (DeepSeek-V3: 2.2-7.4% on high-resource PLs, 7.4% on Lua) and inherent limitation when even high-resource language underperforms, reducing practical impact
Test case generation with only 10 synthetic cases is insufficient for complex problems; no analysis of test quality, coverage, or false positive rates where incorrect code passes synthetic tests

Cross-language serialization protocol (Appendix A.2) with type tags (<N>, <B>) and fixed floating-point tolerance (ε=10⁻⁴) appears ad-hoc; edge cases and language-specific output formats not thoroughly addressed

Evaluation limited primarily to function-level tasks with only brief case study on repository-level code (B.5.4); scope does not cover real-world development scenarios involving language-specific features

Missing critical analyses: no investigation of problem characteristics where transfer succeeds/fails, no discussion of language-pair semantic incompatibilities, no study of when spurious consistency occurs in practice
Variance and confidence intervals not reported for main results; only 5 random seeds for statistical testing; Pass@k analysis missing despite extensive evaluation

Fairness concerns in S* comparison: S* uses iterative adaptive generation (fundamentally different approach); efficiency gains partly from avoiding expensive operations when uncertain, not purely from algorithmic superiority

strengths: Addresses a practical and important problem: improving CodeLLM performance on low-resource programming languages with significant real-world applicability
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple model scales (1.5B-32B), benchmarks, and programming languages with consistent improvements demonstrated
Strong computational efficiency gains: achieves 2× fewer tokens and 4× faster inference compared to S*, a competitive baseline method
Thorough ablation studies examining contributions of multi-temperature sampling, test oracle generation strategies, and adaptive selection mechanism
Honest discussion of limitations and detailed failure analysis showing dependency on source language correctness (Appendix C, Table 13)
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: combines well-established techniques (multi-temperature sampling, majority voting, test-case-guided generation) without introducing novel algorithmic or theoretical insights

Fundamental and underemphasized limitation: method critically depends on high-resource language generating correct implementations; when Python fails, target languages fail 78-97% of the time (Table 13), severely constraining applicability to hard problems

Diminishing returns on stronger models: improvements drop from 23.7% (Qwen-1.5B) to 2.2-7.4% (DeepSeek-V3), with only +5.0% gain even with reasoning-enhanced models (Table 11), questioning long-term relevance

Insufficient justification for design choices: temperature values {0, 0.7, 0.9, 1.1}, clustering thresholds δext=1 and δast=2, and uncertainty indicator K appear somewhat arbitrary without principled motivation or sensitivity analysis

Narrow evaluation scope: almost exclusively function-level algorithmic problems; repository-level claims supported by only one task (B.5.4); generalization to realistic code generation (I/O, language-specific features, idioms) unexplored

Test case generation underexplored: limited analysis of test case quality and discriminativeness; model generates test cases at fixed τ=0.5 rather than optimizing generation; no comparison of alternative strategies

Cross-language test handling involves complex multi-step serialization protocol (A.2) with hardcoded floating-point tolerance (ε=10^-4); edge cases and failure modes not thoroughly analyzed, raising reproducibility concerns

Evaluation design concerns: comparison with S* somewhat unfair (different paradigms); statistical testing relegated to appendix; hyperparameter sensitivity limited; all hyperparameters appear fixed across experiments
Questionable 'training-free' framing: model's knowledge comes from training data; test case generation requires inference compute; distinction from other test-time methods not as clear as presented

Core assumption of functional equivalence via I/O matching oversimplified: does not address numeric precision issues, platform-specific behavior, or language-specific constraints; no exploration of when cross-language transfer is inappropriate

strengths: Addresses a real and important practical problem: the performance gap of CodeLLMs across programming languages, particularly for low-resource languages
Elegant and well-motivated core insight: test cases naturally encapsulate language-agnostic functional knowledge
Uncertainty-aware adaptive selection is a thoughtful design choice that reduces computational overhead while maintaining accuracy (4× faster than S* with better performance)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple dimensions: 4+ benchmarks, 7+ languages, 7+ model variants, consistent improvements (up to 80.6% on Lua)
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating that each component (multi-temperature sampling, test oracle generation, adaptive selection) contributes meaningfully
Strong empirical results with statistical significance testing (p < 0.05) and validation across different model scales
Excellent reproducibility: detailed algorithm pseudocode, prompts provided in appendix, hyperparameter analysis, implementation details including cross-language serialization protocol
Honest and thorough limitations discussion: acknowledges fundamental constraints (dependence on high-resource language quality, reduced benefits for capable models, focus on function-level tasks)
Practical applicability: training-free, immediately deployable to existing systems without retraining
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual components: multi-temperature sampling, test-case guided selection, and majority voting are all well-established techniques; main novelty is the combination with uncertainty-aware routing, which feels somewhat incremental

Fundamental limitation by design: Table 13 shows that when Python reference code fails, other languages fail 78-97% of the time, meaning the method cannot overcome cases where the high-resource language itself struggles
Diminishing improvements for capable models: DeepSeek-V3 gains only 7.4%-2.2%-4.9% on Lua/C++/Java, raising questions about scalability as models improve and cross-language gaps naturally narrow

Theoretical justification could be deeper: while the intuition is appealing, the paper lacks rigorous explanation of why matching Python test outputs should improve low-resource generation and how this differs from single-language execution feedback

Hyperparameter selections lack empirical validation: temperature values (0, 0.7, 0.9, 1.1), sample counts (1, 3, 3, 3), and clustering thresholds (δ_ext=1, δ_ast=2) appear somewhat arbitrary; sensitivity analysis is incomplete

Cross-language output normalization introduces multiple heuristic rules (type tagging, structure unfolding, tolerance-based verification) whose completeness and universality across language pairs is unclear; risk of subtle semantic errors
Limited evaluation of repository-level and complex code generation: paper acknowledges focus on function-level tasks; only one case study (RepoClassBench) provided; scalability uncertain

Missing analysis of when and why transfer is effective: limited exploration of language-pair properties enabling effective transfer; why Python outperforms C++/Java as source (Table 4) not deeply investigated
Test case generation not validated: synthesized test inputs not verified for representativeness, bias, or language-specificity; quality of generated test cases not analyzed

Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing simple transfer baselines (e.g., generate in Python then translate); no comparison with fine-tuning methods for low-resource languages despite mentioning them in related work

Reproducibility gaps: compiler/interpreter versions not specified; custom serialization protocol implementation details potentially incomplete; benchmark-specific handling differences not fully documented
